claims.text: Repeated mechanical wear disrupts the naturally forming protective oxide or passive film on the HEA.
Removal of the passive film exposes microstructurally heterogeneous regions that act as micro-galvanic couples.
Micro-galvanic coupling between phases of differing nobility accelerates localized corrosion.
Wear-induced passive-film disruption followed by micro-galvanic corrosion governs the coupled tribo-corrosion response.
An as-processed HEA can possess a BCC solid-solution matrix together with secondary Laves phases.
The dual-phase HEA normally forms a thin, protective, passivating oxide layer.
Different phases in the heterogeneous microstructure have different passive-film stabilities.
Dual-phase regions become sites of micro-galvanic coupling when the protective oxide is removed.
The exposed phases have contrasting electrochemical potentials.
Electrochemical potential differences between phases produce localized selective dissolution through micro-galvanic coupling.
Micro-galvanic corrosion is concentrated specifically at phase boundaries.
Concurrent wear and corrosion will produce a higher total degradation rate than static corrosion.
Tribo-corrosion will increase corrosion-pit density and depth relative to static corrosion.
The combined material loss will exceed the sum of isolated wear loss and isolated corrosion loss.
Under static corrosion conditions, the HEA can re-establish its passivating oxide layer.
The predicted synergy should occur in passive aqueous environments such as NaCl solution when wear removes the passive film faster than it reforms.
The predicted synergy may be weak or absent in nonpassivating environments or when wear is negligible relative to passive-film reformation.
The magnitude of corrosion acceleration depends on wear frequency and intensity, passive-film reformation kinetics, and compositional heterogeneity.

contradictions.description: The design includes only a combined wear-corrosion condition and a static-corrosion control, but the falsification rule requires determining whether combined loss exceeds the additive effects of isolated wear and isolated corrosion. Without a wear-only control, that additive benchmark cannot be measured decisively.

Wear-track depth is predicted to increase relative to a static-corrosion baseline that undergoes no wear and therefore has no comparable wear track; a wear-only matched baseline is needed for that component.
